title: When Scores Learn Geometry: Rate Separations under the Manifold Hypothesis
claim: Recovering the underlying structure of the data is far easier than recovering its full distribution, with a large gap in required accuracy.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, 3D surface toys above a difficulty curve

abstract: Score-based methods, such as diffusion models and Bayesian inverse problems, are often interpreted as learning the data distribution in the low-noise limit ($Ï\to 0$). In this work, we propose an alternative perspective: their success arises from implicitly learning the data manifold rather than the full distribution. Our claim is based on a novel analysis of scores in the small-$Ï$ regime that reveals a sharp separation of scales: information about the data manifold is $Î(Ï^{-2})$ stronger than information about the distribution. We argue that this insight suggests a paradigm shift from the less practical goal of distributional learning to the more attainable task of geometric learning, which provably tolerates $O(Ï^{-2})$ larger errors in score approximation. We illustrate this perspective through three consequences: i) in diffusion models, concentration on data support can be achieved with a score error of $o(Ï^{-2})$, whereas recovering the specific data distribution requires a much stricter $o(1)$ error; ii) more surprisingly, learning the uniform distribution on the manifold-an especially structured and useful object-is also $O(Ï^{-2})$ easier; and iii) in Bayesian inverse problems, the maximum entropy prior is $O(Ï^{-2})$ more robust to score errors than generic priors. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings with preliminary experiments on large-scale models, including Stable Diffusion.
